en.curator: Visiting al-Zubarah is like travelling back in time. As if in an archaeological laboratory, one is able to walk through its historical past and examine what it was like to live there.
Visiting al-Zubarah is like travelling back in time. As if in an archaeological laboratory, one is able to walk through its historical past and examine what it was like to live there.

The ruins of Carthage represent milestones in the history of humanity: of significant personalities, events and creative endeavours (Queen Dido, Aeneas, the *Aeneid*, Rome, Hannibal, Cato, Roman generals and emperors, Christian bishops, Arab caliphs, and Phoenician, Roman and Islamic cultures). The ruins are the physical embodiments of the collective memory, of a long-gone ancient culture, economy and life, and the intertwining layers of human history.

One of Jordan’s most significant heritage sites, it demonstrates the coexistence of different cultures and societies in one urban space.

The lithograph, which illustrates a site of great archaeological significance, points to a scientific as well as an aesthetic interest in the ancient past. Besides its importance to archaeological studies, artworks such as this were used as reference by artists, designers and architects.

Studies of different sites are valuable as documents of the urban assets of a city, immortalising it in visual documents at a specific point in time. This lithograph was made at a time when Athens was collating its urban assets. As the first king of Greece following independence from the Ottoman Empire, King Otto wanted to remodel the city and breathe new “new life” into it by recalling the city’s classical past.

The Hippodrome was one of the main centres of city life in this capital city of the ancient world, Byzantium (then Constantinople). Here, where magnificent works of ancient Egypt, Greek, and Rome are found together, the intertwining layers of time and cultures up until the Ottoman era are revealed.
Every period has left its mark on this site, which has changed ownership many times over the centuries. The building can be read as an architectural-historical look into the past.
Studying this plan of ancient Troy, based on the excavations by Heinrich Schliemann, it is possible to gain a picture of the urban structure of the ancient city.
Urban sites can be studied using maps that depict topographic features, or archaeological sites and their finds.
This photo is a rare representation of work-in-progress, showing the construction process of the Dolmabahçe Palace.

This photo depicts the growth of settlements and the characteristics of the residential areas along the bank of the river. It provides details of the location and the connection between the watercourse and the mainland (the boat and the lighthouse) and also suggests the different building types that are on the banks of the river and the surrounding landscape.

The creation of open, green public spaces such as parks and gardens is central to urban planning. The Sanayeh Garden, commissioned by Khalil Pasha and a manifestation of Ottoman power and planning, is one of the oldest public parks in Beirut.
A main site of traditional city life that manifests national identity through its form and style.

The mosque represents the core identity of Islamic architecture, a building dedicated to God. Built under the patronage of a royal woman in the old commercial centre of the city, the site also attracted business and trade activities between Muslim and non-Muslim merchants, representing another important layer in the identity of Istanbul.

An aquatint depicting the famous Café du Marabout, a vestige of the many that once furnished Arab and Ottoman cities, and which step-by-step Europeans embraced, turning them into fashionable venues for the elite. Cafés are important social spaces in the Arab and Ottoman world that are mainly frequented by men.

The engraving focuses on some of the most important identifying factors of Damascus: the mosque complex represents piety, Islam as the basis of an individual’s life as well as the community’s; the merchants symbolise a strong global presence in trade and economics; the Ottoman-style buildings represent the power of the Empire; and the new French-built road signifies the city’s modern era.
Depicting one of the oldest and most important universities of the Islamic world, this painting illustrates some salient features of Cairene identity: local history, tradition and lifestyle.
Built in the Ottoman style, the design and structure of the Citadel of Cairo symbolises Ottoman power and the new ruler.
The style of this building represents the rediscovery of Portugal’s Arabian past and also hosts one of the country’s most significant social events and traditions, the bullfight.
The style of this building represents the rediscovery of Portugal’s Arabian past and also hosts one of the country’s most significant social events and traditions, the bullfight.
The style of this building represents the rediscovery of Portugal’s Arabian past and also hosts one of the country’s most significant social events and traditions, the bullfight.

The monument can be considered as an expression of the symbolic interconnections between the three main pillars of Syrian society in the era: political identity (Ottoman Sultan ‘Abd al-Hamid presenting Islam as a unifying factor); modernity (the telegraph system); and religious values (the Islamic *hajj* and the Holy Cities of Mecca and Medina).
The square, which is an important meeting point for the local population in the centre of Tunis, holds an important transnational monument.

The image depicts the daily life of an Arab city-dweller to illustrate Arab culture and handicrafts to the reader of Charles Lallemand’s *Tunis et ses environs*. The “Eastern” style had a huge impact on European arts and crafts.

The image of the “East”, seen in intimate interiors such as this, was one circulated throughout Europe. It inspired not only European art and fashion, but also the tradition of identifying cultures through architecture, ornament, decoration and costume or fashion.

The innovation of steam-engine technology, following Thomas Newcomen and James Watt, revolutionised the industrial sector. Installing a high-tech machine in a building form that in the Arab and Ottoman world is associated with sacred spaces perhaps not only celebrated the vogue for the “East”, but also in some way elevated the Industrial Revolution beyond the daily and profane.

Looking like a small palace set beside town houses, the pumping station turns to face the world. The smoke seen coming from the chimney suggests that the photo was taken when the pumping station was at the peak of its operation.
The first railway station in Lebanon followed the style of small European railway stations of the 19th century.

With its Neoclassical architectural style and painted decoration, the train station says a lot about the impact of European taste on late 19th- and early 20th-century architecture in the Ottoman city. Presented by Emperor Wilhelm II as a gift the building, constructed by German architects for a German-owned company, represents Germany’s “drive to East”. Situated on the bank of the Bosphorus the building can be understood as a symbolic gateway, not only to the coast, but to the great Ottoman lands that stretched all the way to Baghdad.
Financed by foreign companies, the railway station at Skopje followed the style of small central European railway stations of the 19th century.

Evoking a Venetian palace, but with traditional Arab and Ottoman architecture behind the façade, this structure was built for Hijaz Railways. Standing at one end of the pilgrimage route to Mecca, at its peak this was one of the most important and busy stations of the Arab and Ottoman world.

An important station on the Hijaz Railway, Amman represents the political and cross-cultural connections of the Ottoman Empire with Germany and also signifies the power and political claims of the Ottomans over the territory.
A small but strategically important station along the Hijaz Railway, the station was constructed from local materials and built in the European architectural style.

The last station on the route of the Orient Express, Tripoli holds an important role in the modern transport infrastructure of Lebanon. In terms of the form and decoration of the building, the influence of European architecture is apparent.

An elegant form of Tunisian colonial architecture, the theatre was designed by a French architect using the vocabulary of European architecture, a style which many public theatres built after it followed.
The factory-worker class gave birth to workers’ associations, societies and unions, and also buildings such as this one in simple architectural forms.
An imposing 19th-century Neoclassical opera house built as the tradition was flourishing in Europe and to serve the European community living abroad.
The building was built in the Neoclassical style to match 19th-century European counterparts.
Factory buildings are one of the most significant features of the Industrial Revolution. This building was commissioned by a royal patron and served as a centre for tile production.
This quintessentially Ottoman-style building was erected during the empire’s rule. The infirmary provided medical care to military personnel.
A 19th-century public school run by missionaries, the architecture is traditionally Lebanese with European influences.
Evoking a European fortified palace façade on a hilltop, the building represented a new educational form in Lebanon.
The building, commissioned by the Jesuits in the European style, heralded the introduction of higher education in Arab and Ottoman lands.
Astronomy has a long tradition in Portugal due to the country’s maritime prowess, but governmental astronomical observatories were a 19th-century phenomenon.
This Neoclassical building, purpose-built to house a museum, shows the influence of the British architect Robert Adam.

The museum, which was founded during the 19th century at a time when many Arab, Ottoman and Southern Mediterranean countries were founding public museums in parallel with European counterparts, was constructed in the “canonised” Neoclassical style that evoked ancient Greek classical architecture.

The revolution in communications brought about the construction of this building to serve the postal service. Its importance is due to the fact that it represents the First National Style in Ottoman architecture. It was designed by a local architect who studied in France and whose work manifests the cultural connections between the empire and France at this time.

The requirement for luxury among the travelling elite brought the hotel construction business to the fore. This hotel is built in a style typical of this era of luxury hotels for Europeans in Arab and Ottoman lands.

The vogue for travel on the Orient Express called for the construction of a new luxury hotel to accommodate its wealthy passengers. By using the vocabulary of European architecture and ensuring that all the “luxuries of home” were available, guests felt immediately comfortable.
Bridges symbolise connections between places as well as historical eras. This one was built using modern construction methods and materials.
The presence of a new-style housing structure is significant, as are the additional city gates and the modern tramlines.

The square is testament to the building activities of Isma‘il Pasha under whose patronage residences for foreign consuls were built around the square. The square became the heart of Ottoman diplomacy with Europeans and a hub of Alexandria’s trade (the Bourse). Focusing on the square’s European-style arrangement and residences, it was designed by a French architect to evoke the style of Europe and the statue in the background is by a French sculptor.

This square is a significant example for the West’s encounter with local life and traditions: the offices for trade were located on the ground- and first floors near the harbour; foreign consulates were accommodated on the upper floors and were able to make use of an inner courtyard, which in the style of the traditional *khan*\-system, they could use for parking their carriages and resting their horses.
A European-style square where tramlines and carriages, landscape architecture, European-style buildings and a mosque are all evidence of the historic-cum-modernist vocabulary of public space.

A European-style figurative statue stands prominently in a public square. The buildings around the square suggest how the traditional Arab‒Ottoman architectural style was absorbed by the contemporary European style.

The clock tower, which was a new addition to the skyline in Arab and Ottoman cities, symbolically marked the importance of the daily routine in the ever-burgeoning, more industrialised world of trade and commercial activity.
Railways and railway stations were the focal point of transport networks and the city.
Tripoli Railway Station comprises elements that are familiar in the local architectural tradition and others that are borrowed from modern European architecture.

The Post Office became the landmark of the new era. Istanbul’s main Post Office was designed by local architect Vedat Tek in the First National Style of Ottoman architecture and was constructed between 1903 and 1909.

Christian places of worship are important elements in the structure of Arab and Ottoman cities. The style of this church belongs with the European Gothic Revival, but refers symbolically to the era of the Crusades.
A historic map of the city and harbour.
A survey map representing the social and economic web and interrelations in a district of Beirut.
A map showing the presence of a foreign community and the space they inhabited within the city’s texture.
A map that shows new public services and illustrates the impact of new technologies in the region.
A map documenting the harbour after modernisation.
A view of Algiers from the sea, identifying its different rural and urban sections and skyline.
A colour view of Constantinople that shows various sections of the city and the skyline dominated by domes and towers.
A panorama of Cairo, focusing on the Citadel Mosque, showing how it altered the balance of the surrounding city, and also how the proliferation of tall minarets dominated the city’s skyline.
Admiring this photograph, one is also able to study the topography, structure and some of the main building-types of Istanbul.
A panoramic view of the city with the skyline determined by the shapes of mosques and minarets.

A photo from 1920, which represents a European “vision” for Casablanca, where many transnational influences can be seen. French investors, who considered the city as a sort of architectural laboratory, experimented with the skyline there.
A colour lithograph showing a historic view of Algiers.

As one of the grandest buildings on the square, it determines and dominates the view of the square and helps to separate it from the rest of the city’s neighbourhood. Designed by a European architect, the building reveals so-called colonial architectural features along with local and European design elements.
A plan of Oran, Algeria, depicting the different sections and parts of its urban system.

The *mashrabiyya*, made from stone, glass or wood and seen throughout the Middle East and Southern Mediterranean countries, represents an important social observation: the separation of public and private space, seen ubiquitously in the architecture of the traditional Arab house.

Glazed tiles were used widely in the Arab and Ottoman world to decorate buildings or garden structures. Many specific types of glaze in different colours and a variety of motifs were used. This piece, which is decorated with geometrical motifs and has an inscription, was made in Kütahya.

This glazed panel, decorated with floral ornaments, was used to decorate a mosque. Tiles are significant design elements, not only as part of the building’s fixtures and fittings, but for the motifs used on them as well.
This tympanum was used to decorate the space above a door. Its type, form, material and decoration are all important elements of Ottoman art and architectural design.

This mosque represents many important design elements of Islamic architecture: its square-shaped minaret is similar to minarets of the Muslim West; the walls are decorated with green *zellij*; and the roof tiles have both a decorative and functional role.
The form of the garden is notable as is the relationship between the garden and the murals.

As so-called “great-scale” elements of urban design, mosque domes and minarets are considered two of the most distinct features of Arab and Ottoman cities. However, they are also the most significant as they determine the texture of the city and its skyline: the curved shapes of domes contrasting with the upright, vertical shapes of minarets, which like elegant exclamation marks stand within the complex mass of the mosque complex and the surrounding city.

This photo, taken by the studio of Abdullah Frères, immortalises the Dolmabahçe Mosque that enriched the Istanbul skyline in the 19th century. It was designed by the famous Balyan family of architects, whose work integrates Ottoman architecture with elements of European Baroque, Rococo, Neoclassical and Empire style, and even uses some from the Chinese and Indian traditions.

Domes and minarets, as basic design elements of Arab and Ottoman architecture, appear in European buildings of the 19th and early 20th century. This example illustrates the interface and connection between the art of Europe and the influence of Arab and Ottoman art in Italy, where elements of Arab‒Ottoman architecture entered by way of the popularity of the “Liberty style” and Eclecticism.

Public fountains are among the most important elements of Arab and Ottoman urban design and play a special role in most European cities as well. This elegant example, which has a mosque-like decoration at the top with a dome and two minarets, is made from marble, a material frequently used in Arab and Ottoman architecture.

Throughout the Arab and Ottoman world, fountains are important design elements in private and public gardens, courtyards, and public squares. This water fountain was used in Ottoman *majlis* (councils) in Lebanon. The external walls are covered with a marble mosaic of different shapes and sizes and colours to create geometric patterns, which is a very particular design element of the Arab and Ottoman world.

Public fountains are important urban design elements in the Arab and Ottoman world that are often built by royal patronage to provide a public water source. Fountains hold special significance in most European cities as well, where often they are built through the patronage of a royal or papal procurer.

Clock towers, once they were introduced from Europe, became a fairly ubiquitous design element of Arab and Ottoman cities. Besides providing an eye-catching focal element in the city view, they also served a practical purpose: to mark time and underline the importance of routine in the ever-burgeoning, more industrialised world of trade and commercial activity. This clock tower is a manifestation not only of traditional architecture and ornamentation from various provenances of Turkey and beyond, but also a re-rendition, by a French architect, who reintroduced it into the recaptured city of the Ottoman Empire.

An example of the interconnected design elements of traditional Arab and Ottoman art and architecture: the walls are high and windowless to protect the privacy of its inhabitants; a delicately carved, openwork alcove or *mashrabiyya* projects above the entrance portal, which allows air and light into the room behind it and provides those within the chance to observe outside life discreetly from within.
The Ortaköy Mosque demonstrates the intertwining elements of traditional Arab and Ottoman design and form and European art and architecture: a neo-baroque building decorated with a dome and minarets.

The obelisk immortalises and glorifies the king, with representations praising his acts. Erected during a civil war, the monument pays homage to the king’s power and is a reminder to the people of the power and the glory of the country under his reign.

One of the obelisks was originally erected to venerate Pharaoh Thutmose III, while its relocation to the Hippodrome glorified the reign and the power of the Roman Emperor Theodosius the Great; and since under his rule the state religion became Orthodox Nicene Christianity, also to promote the Orthodox Christian faith. The other obelisk was erected to immortalise the power of Constantinus Porphyrogenitus and the Christian faith.

Part of the magnificent Parthian Monument, the frieze was erected as a tribute the Antonine Roman Emperors. Commissioned to honour Lucius Verus and Marcus Aurelius, it also represented the legitimisation of their dynastic lineage through adoptions.

These bronze figures of athletes of the Apoxymenos (Apoksimene) type were erected to pay tribute to the human body and its victorious efforts. Statues of athletes were commissioned to commemorate Olympic champions.
Commemorating his victorious military campaigns and his reign, Emperor Hadrian is depicted here as a glorious and majestic ruler and general of the military, nemesis of the enemies of the Empire.
Triumphal arches are perhaps the most significant and powerful memories erected to commemorate or pay tribute to a victorious and glorious human being.
The Eiffel Tower was erected to glorify and commemorate the 1889 World’s Fair in Paris, the theme of which was to commemorate the 100th anniversary of the French Revolution.
The statue of Jules Ferry, a former Prime Minister of France and a strong supporter of French colonialism in Africa, once stood on the Place d’Afrique in Tunis as a symbol of the French Protectorate.

One of the most powerful symbols and manifestations of the Christian faith and its communities in the Arab and Ottoman territories, the Lady of Harissa represents the Virgin Mary’s solicitude, her outstretched arms protecting the people of Harissa and all of Lebanon.

At one of Tunisia’s most important 19th-century public squares is a statue of Cardinal Lavigerie, Archbishop of Carthage and Algiers and Primate of Africa, to commemorate his missionary works and his efforts to end the slave trade.

A jewel of 19th-century fountain architecture in Istanbul, this elaborate freestanding fountain commemorates the acts, the reign and the dynasty of Valide Sultan Saliha; in terms of its structure, which follows earlier prototypes, it is also a reminder of the history, legacy and continuity of the Ottoman Empire; and in terms of its function, it represents the pious act of the gift of sweet water to the public.
The clock tower commemorates and glorifies Ottoman rule and the reign of Sultan ‘Abd al-Hamid II in Beirut, Lebanon.

The clock tower was erected to glorify and commemorate the reign, dynasty and personality of Sultan ‘Abd al-Hamid II. Designed by a French architect and displaying a clock presented by the German Emperor Wilhelm II, it also signifies European ideals and cultural interests, not least the political connections of the Sultan.
The clock tower signals modernity and European influences, but as it was erected to pay tribute to Sultan ‘Abd al-Hamid II, it also symbolises Ottoman rule and hegemony in Tripoli.
As a tribute to modernity and Ottoman hegemony, the clock tower commemorates the anniversary of the reign of Sultan ‘Abd al-Hamid II.
Its presence, particularly at this location, symbolises 19th-century Ottoman hegemony, but it also pays tribute to the technical achievements of humankind and thus celebrates modernity.
The map depicts different sections of the city according to diverse social, cultural, economic, public and private purposes.
A new map-form that depicts the trade and commerce facilities of Beirut.
A topographic view to show the commercial and cultural sites and districts of Smyrna.

The water supply system of course is fundamental to the city plan. Fountains are not only functional but have recreational and aesthetic appeal as well: the Neo-Mudéjar decoration of this fountain appeals to a commonly shared history and national identity.
This view of the Port documents work in progress.
Both the position and the architectural features of the Bank are designed to represent the power and stability of the Ottoman Empire.
A map to document the structure and system of the Port of Beirut after expansion.

The location, height and architectural features of the Bourse ensured the building’s landmark status in modern Alexandria. The impact of European architecture is clear, but it seems appropriate to the building’s function as well.
While the Neo-Manueline style in Portugal reminded the Portuguese people of their Manueline past it also reflected the contemporary vogue for Romantic architecture.
The city gate serves a functional and aesthetic purpose, but it has a symbolic meaning as well, as a confine between rural and urban life and culture.

The monument is a prominent landmark, symbolising the municipal administration and also embodying a strong political message. The bronze column, erected at the centre of Merje Square, was designed to represent the power and greatness of the Ottoman Empire.

At the heart of the Citadel complex, a manifestation of Ottoman power in an ancient Arab city, there is an Ottoman-style mosque, which – together with the nearby palace – also incorporates modern architectural structures.
An Arab urban design reference to the 1840s in Istanbul.

While working in Istanbul, D’Aronco increased his knowledge of local architectural traditions and building techniques. This influenced his work, signalling more of a cultural exchange than a one-way impact. Among his works in Istanbul are the Yıldız Palace Theatre, the Yıldız Palace Island Kiosk, the Yıldız Palace Small State Kiosk and the Italian Embassy in Tarabya.

While working in Istanbul, D’Aronco increased his knowledge of local architectural traditions and building techniques. This influenced his work, signalling more of a cultural exchange than a one-way impact. Among his works in Istanbul are the Yıldız Palace Theatre, the Yıldız Palace Island Kiosk, the Yıldız Palace Small State Kiosk and the Italian Embassy in Tarabya.

A furniture shop with impressive Islamic and Western design influences, it illustrates the cultural dialogue between Europe and the Arab and Ottoman world. The shop further enhanced its national identity through the types, forms and styles of the household furniture it sold.
The Politeama Rossini Theatre was built under the patronage of an Italian construction company and designed by a European architect. It represents the introduction of European modernism in Tunis.

The Lincoln Hotel was built in 1916 for the increasing number of European tourists to the city. Designed by a French architect, the hotel is an eclectic mix of Arab and al-Andalus architecture, it also illustrates the impact of European architectural styles in the era.

The construction of this building stretches across two decades, from its design during the first decade of the 1900s to its completion in 1927. Designed by a Frenchman, the building is a harmonious combination of European architectural features and the traditions of local art and architecture.

Commissioned by an Italian company and designed by the Italian architect G. di Vittorio, the building has features of traditional Ottoman architecture. As an important site of local city life, the Bazaar betrays European design influences and represents Western political power in the Tunisian capital.

This small building in the Ottoman capital is a compilation of European revivalist features, mostly elements from Mannerism and the Baroque. The interior decoration shows evidence of European craftsmanship and has elements designed specifically to suit the Western lifestyle.
During its most recent modification in the early 20th century, the reconstruction featured elements of Roman architecture and Early Greek Christian architecture as historical points of reference.
The interior of the mosque comprises a rich and colourfully decorated round central hall. Various general maxims are inscribed in Arabic and translated into German.
The interior of the mosque comprises a rich and colourfully decorated round central hall. Various general maxims are inscribed in Arabic and translated into German.

During reconstruction of the “Moorish Kiosk” the colour scheme was redesigned entirely. An abundant use of gold was considered not only as a symbol of royalty but also thought to be a “Moorish” element. Coloured glazing, “in the Moorish style”, and a tessellated floor were introduced to underline the Ottoman character of the house.

During reconstruction of the “Moorish Kiosk” the colour scheme was redesigned entirely. An abundant use of gold was considered not only as a symbol of royalty but also thought to be a “Moorish” element. Coloured glazing, “in the Moorish style”, and a tessellated floor were introduced to underline the Ottoman character of the house.

The complex, which having its roots in the traditional *külliye* system comprises a mosque, mausoleum, *sabil* (water dispensary), fountain, clock-room and school, was built in the eclectic style, bringing together elements from European Gothic, Ottoman, Islamic and Indian arts and architecture. Note the bronze chandelier in the 19th-century European style.

A fascinating structure that elegantly celebrates elements of Arab and Ottoman art and architecture. Situated on a bay of the Havel River it adds a picturesque architectural accent to the Potsdam cultural landscape. Behind the façade, which is designed to look like a mosque, steam technology at the highest level for the era produces 81.4 horsepower to drive the fountains at the Sanssouci Palace.

In the tradition of Italian villa architecture, Villa Crespi was designed in the “Moorish” style as a countryside residence for an Italian businessman. It expresses the patron’s admiration for Baghdad and Arab and Ottoman art and architecture in general.
Elaborate tile panels feature large in Arab and Ottoman art and architecture. Techniques and motifs from this tradition inspired the work of William Morris, as seen in this bathroom tile.

The glazed tile or *azulejo* is a particularly expressive component of Portuguese art and architecture. Relating to the period of the Moors in Portugal, it also links with the Arab and Ottoman tradition of tile design and production.
Ruins of a *nymphaeum* ‒ the ancient Greek and Roman sites consecrated to water nymphs ‒ and its temple.

The construction of the Temple of Bacchus (Dionysius) is evidence that the cult spread throughout the Roman Empire. The empire’s conversion to Christianity in the 4th century saw an end to temples dedicated to this god.
One of the most ancient sites of religious worship is that of the Temple of Baal, a Canaanite god.

The Temple of Karnak is the world’s largest religious complex and the Hypostyle hall still the largest room inside any religious building. The temple was dedicated to Amon, Mut and Khonsu, the Theban triad of Egyptian gods.
The temple is one of the main features of ancient Egyptian religion, a fundamental part of the social structure and theocracy: the belief that the pharaohs are incarnations of Gods.
Ruins of the Temple of Horus from the Ptolemaic period in Egypt.
Since they are the burial sites of pharaohs, the pyramids are religious monuments.
The most important religious site of the Islamic faith, all faithful Muslims aspire to visit Mecca, the Ka’aba and the sacred complex that surrounds it at least once in a lifetime.
Important ruins of the Great Abbasid Mosque with its unique type of minaret.
This mosque and mausoleum, commemorating an important Muslim imam, is a most significant religious site in Lebanon.
The tomb is visited by many people who come out of respect and to remember.
A mosque and shrine dedicated to a sacred man.
Late Ottoman religious architecture by a local architect that shows fluid transformation of the European architectural vocabulary into the local architectural language.
Integrating Ottoman mosque constructions and European architectural influences, the ornamental decoration is based on a dialogue of colours.

The façade appears as if it were lace or net frozen in stone. A magnificent example of late 19th-century Ottoman mosque architecture, built under the patronage of a royal woman, it provides a unique example of the incorporation of architectural styles from different eras and cultures, European and Indian, based on the local Ottoman architectural vocabulary.

The impact of European architecture is apparent in the Neo-Baroque façade of this 19th-century Ottoman mosque on the Bosphorus. It was commissioned by Sultan Abdülmecid and designed by Armenian architects.
Puritan, humble and simple architectural construction, this late 19th-century church is a reminder of structures from early European Christianity.
The church, which was built for the Greek Orthodox community of Tunis by a locally based Italian architect, represents a revival of traditional Orthodox church architecture in the early 20th century.

The cathedral is a fine example of the transformation of the traditional Arab architectural language to accommodate European Gothic traditions. Designed by an Italian architect, it illustrates early 20th-century local architecture of the Maronite community, built using local materials.
The style of this multi-ethnic church, founded in the second half of the 19th century, evokes late Roman European-style church architecture.

The presence of the Capuchin missionaries in Beirut is documented from 1655. From its name, this church can be traced to one of the main saints of France, who also happens to be one of the most significant saint-kings of the Roman Catholic Church. A revival of the late Roman‒early Gothic style, it was built using locally available materials.

The method of construction, location and source of inspiration for this building of the Maronite community manifests a significant spiritual and cultural message. The nationality of its architect being Italian, symbolically, the cathedral attests to both late 19th-century cross-cultural relations between Italy and the Arab and Ottoman world and the connection between the Maronite and Roman Catholic Church as well.

This landmark Greek Orthodox Church in Lebanon is the oldest church building still extant in Beirut. Its late 19th‒early 20th-century remodelling, which harmoniously added a Late Roman-style portico, also embellished the building with Neo-Byzantine style frescoes.

This centre for Lebanese-Greek Catholics in Beirut is a further example of the revivalist style of the second half of the 19th century. The imposing Neo-Byzantine exterior not only protects a magnificent Neo-Gothic interior, but also reveals the impact of traditional Arab architecture. Its reconstruction in the 20th century is a significant example of the protection of the local heritage in Lebanon.

Materially, the building follows local forms, making use of limestone and sandstone; stylistically, it harks back to the Gothic period, perhaps one of the most significant eras for the construction of Christian churches. It is a good example of the 19th-century Gothic Revival and represents culturally the presence of non-Roman Catholic Christian churches in Arab and Ottoman lands.

Villa-type architecture is rooted in Italian architectural history, but here this style has been innovatively evoked while also reflecting the aesthetic of Arab and Ottoman architecture. A building inspired by the art and architecture of Baghdad, the minaret being one of the main architectural features, it has made use of many 19th-century technical developments as well. A small so-called “company town” was constructed near the Crespi factory and villa.
With its construction, façades and decoration, the house is a good example of Macedonian urban architecture.
Built to accommodate a steam engine, a main force of the Industrial Revolution, this building was the result of international cooperation.

The majestic station building integrates elements of Arab‒Ottoman architectural vocabulary with European architectural elements. The railway revolutionised travel to the Holy Site of Mecca so that thousands more Islamic pilgrims had access to it; symbolically, of course, it also celebrated Ottoman power in Syria.
The hotel was built to accommodate European tourists, but also as a show of British power in the area.
The hotel, designed by a Frenchman during the French Protectorate, displays features of Moorish revival architecture.
The architectural style, materials and location of the building all demonstrate the influence, power and presence of the French Protectorate in Tunis.

The Palace of the Poste Italienne was a manifestation of Italy’s power and presence in Alexandria. Here the building is in ruins after “anti-foreign rioting”, marking a change in the political climate.
This fascinating town-palace, now a museum, incorporates local Lebanese architecture with European.

The former palace, which has two wings located at either side of a garden, follows local architectural traditions. Opened as a public museum in 1915, it was one of the first public museums to be founded in the country.

The school was founded in response to new ideas and methods in teaching and in relation to the education of girls. Established in the 19th century, the architecture blends European styles with local traditions.
Following the canons of European architecture, the building was built as a higher education institution for priests of the Greek-Catholic community.

In a typical patriarchal house in which a cohabitating extended family lived, the inhabitants’ social status was reflected within the inner spaces. Its orientation (the main façade faces north), small apertures and an inner courtyard are all designed to keep the interior cool.

The more humble sectors of Islamic society lived in dwellings designed to house people and domestic animals under the same roof. With small apertures in the dense walls, the house was used mostly as a secure place to rest, with most other family activities taking place outside the house.
A typical Lebanese house, built using local materials, and painted in a traditional colour. The architecture is adapted to keep the inhabitants cool and meet their everyday needs.

A typical Lebanese house, seen in both rural and urban contexts, where farmers and the less affluent among society lived. This small house is purely functional: built from local materials, it has only small apertures in the walls.

A traditional Lebanese house in an urban setting, built out of locally sourced materials in the traditional way, but with its façade turned towards the street. Now the core of the inner spaces for family gatherings is a big hall inside the house.

An old-style house-type in Istanbul made out of stone and brick and typically painted red. Closed balconies are oriented towards narrow streets, and wooden structures and carved latticework, along with *mashrabiyya*, protect privacy, shut out bright sunlight and provide ventilation.
Built using local materials, the architectural appearance of this typical Macedonian house indicates some influence of Western designs: small, shuttered windows that open out to the street.
A typical Macedonian house, built out of locally sourced stone and wood, but showing the impact of Arab and Ottoman architecture.

A traditional type of dwelling, built from either limestone or sandstone, and showing the typical type of house that a relatively poor family would have inhabited. In this communal-type house, families from other houses, often from the same geographic origins, would share one courtyard.
An example of a 19th-century Lebanese house that shows influences from European architecture: the surface of the façade, ironwork and the stucco decoration.
A Lebanese building-type, based on traditional models, but showing the impact of European architecture on Ottoman modernity following new building regulations in Ottoman lands.

A traditional house-type of the Macedonian region built from local stone and wood. Almost totally closed to the outside, the dwelling minimises the uses of windows and doorways and manifests its intention to provide defence and shelter to the inhabitants.
A significant example of a traditional urban Macedonian house.
A traditional Lebanese house built in wood, but showing influences from European architecture.

The *wikalat* is a typical urban collective-type dwelling.
A 19th-century Ottoman summer palace showing European architectural influence.
The impact of European architectural styles can be seen in traditional Lebanese house-building and construction.
A typical private house of the Reka area, built by local craftsmen, who made masterly use of local materials.
A significant example of the Debar-Reka school of regional architecture.
Traditional houses responded to the challenges of the local climate.
A typical example of Ottoman communal-type dwellings during the 19th-century.

A residence commissioned by Sultan Abdülmecid I, the Palace was built facing Europe on the European side of the Bosphorus. Its style reveals the sultan’s taste and passion for European art and architecture (the baroque, rococo and neoclassical vocabulary) and also his respect for Ottoman palace architecture.
A town-palace constructed for a prince, which was built using local materials and in an Ottoman style, but also borrowed from the architectural vocabulary of Europe’s past and present.
